title: Beyond poverty: Why growing the middle class is a different challenge
gist: A new World Bank paper on East Asia and Pacific finds roughly one in three people now belong to an economically secure middle class -- driven overwhelmingly by China's rise from 11% to ~40% middle-class share between 2010-2021 -- but momentum has slowed elsewhere as productivity growth stalls, workers displaced from agriculture land in low-productivity services rather than manufacturing, and robot/AI adoption is bifurcating the labor market into skilled winners and displaced low-skilled routine workers.

themes.theme: China dominates the region's middle-class growth story

insights.claim: About one in three people in the East Asia and Pacific region now belong to a middle class with enough economic security to withstand shocks without falling back into poverty, and the region leads the world in the pace of middle-class growth over the last decade.
insights.speaker: Lalita Moorty
insights.so_what: A one-third middle-class share signals a large and still-expanding consumer base in the region, relevant for consumer-facing and services investment theses.
insights.locator: Today, roughly one in three people in the EAP region belongs to the middle class

insights.claim: China's middle class grew from 11 percent of the population in 2010 to around 40 percent in 2021, and this growth accounts for much of the region's overall middle-class expansion, while momentum has slowed across the rest of East Asia and Pacific.
insights.speaker: Lalita Moorty
insights.so_what: Regional middle-class growth narratives are disproportionately a China story; investors should not extrapolate China's consumer-class trajectory onto the rest of Southeast Asia without adjustment.
insights.locator: Much of this has been driven by China

insights.claim: Urban residents in the East Asia and Pacific region are twice as likely as rural residents to belong to the middle class, even though rural areas have also seen strong progress, making cities the region's primary engines of upward mobility.
insights.speaker: Lalita Moorty
insights.so_what: Urbanization rate and city-level infrastructure investment remain a key leading indicator for consumer-class expansion and demand growth in the region.
insights.locator: EAP's cities remain the most powerful engines of upward mobility

themes.theme: Jobs engine is stalling on productivity

insights.claim: Around 77 percent of upper-income earners and 59 percent of the middle class in EAP hold salaried jobs, versus the poor and vulnerable who remain concentrated in agriculture, unpaid work, and self-employment -- sectors that rarely provide enough security to enable an escape into the middle class.
insights.speaker: Sailesh Tiwari
insights.so_what: Salaried formal employment remains the primary vehicle for middle-class formation in the region; formalization rate is a useful proxy metric for tracking future middle-class growth.
insights.locator: Jobs have been the single most powerful driver of middle-class expansion

insights.claim: Labor productivity in most EAP economies outside China and Malaysia remains below the global average and its growth is slowing, with workers leaving agriculture moving primarily into low-productivity services rather than the high-productivity manufacturing that historically drove middle-class expansion.
insights.speaker: Sailesh Tiwari
insights.so_what: This is a structural break from the classic Asian development playbook (agriculture-to-manufacturing ladder); investors should discount the assumption that EAP economies will replicate China's manufacturing-led middle-class formation.
insights.locator: Labor productivity remains below the global average in most economies

insights.claim: Robot adoption across five major EAP economies created around 2 million jobs for skilled formal workers between 2018 and 2022 while displacing 1.4 million low-skilled workers in routine manual roles, for a net gain of 600,000 jobs that masks a stark bifurcation between winners and losers.
insights.speaker: Sailesh Tiwari
insights.so_what: The headline net-jobs figure hides that automation is eliminating exactly the low-skill entry points that historically served as the first rung into the formal economy -- a warning for policymakers and labor-intensive manufacturers relying on that entry-level workforce.
insights.quote: The net figure of 600,000 jobs sounds positive until you look at who is on each side of the ledger
insights.locator: The World Bank's Future Jobs report finds that robot adoption

insights.claim: Digital platforms have expanded labor market access for women through e-commerce and drawn younger, mostly male workers into gig work, but this platform work rarely comes with health coverage, pensions, or job security even when pay is comparable to other informal work.
insights.speaker: Sailesh Tiwari
insights.so_what: Platform/gig-economy growth in EAP should not be read as genuine middle-class formation without accompanying portable social-protection reform.
insights.locator: Digital platforms have opened real doors

themes.theme: Policy prescription for durable middle-class growth

insights.claim: The paper argues sustained middle-class growth requires acting on three fronts simultaneously: investing in human capital (education, health, training that complements new technology), expanding economic opportunity via infrastructure/business environment/private capital, and extending portable social protection benefits to informal workers who make up the majority of the region's workforce.
insights.speaker: Lalita Moorty
insights.so_what: A three-pronged policy checklist investors and development finance institutions can use to evaluate which EAP countries are structurally positioned for durable consumer-class growth versus those stalling.
insights.locator: Meeting this challenge calls for action on three fronts simultaneously

insights.claim: The middle class is framed as both the consuming class that drives domestic demand independent of exports and a political constituency that demands better public services and contributes more to financing them, strengthening the social contract.
insights.speaker: Lalita Moorty
insights.so_what: Middle-class expansion is framed as a self-reinforcing growth driver for domestic demand, an argument for weighting consumer-facing and services investment in economies with rising middle-class shares.
insights.locator: the middle class is also the consuming class
